events.title: Shein, Temu shoppers keep adding to cart despite environmental concerns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ultra-fast fashion buyers feel a lack of personal responsibility despite environmental concerns A new study of ultra-fast fashion buyers found price was one of the biggest shopping motivators. ( AP: Richard Drew ) Shoppers of ultra-fast fashion companies, such as Shein and Temu, say despite being aware of environmental and ethical concerns other factors such as price, convenience and not feeling personally responsible keep them coming back. A new study published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing this week found millennials, who frequently expressed concern about ethical and sustainability issues, often did not translate this concern into purchasing behaviour. The study surveyed 20 Australian millennials who shopped on ultra-fast fashion sites about what informed their purchasing behaviours. It found affordability, convenience, promotions, social media trends, novelty, variety and social validation were the biggest purchase drivers. For some, affordability meant they were likely to purchase styles they may not usually try and make riskier choices. You can get five things for the price of one at other places. I can redo my wardrobe every season without hurting my bank account. It's perfect when I need something quick and cheap for an event. The study also found the purchases were usually not spontaneous, with many shoppers saying they saved carts and waited for a sale before purchasing. When I see a 70 per cent off notification, it's almost impossible not to look. It feels like I'm losing money if I don't buy it. Sales get me every time. I've bought outfits I didn't even wear just because they were on sale. I add things to my cart and wait for payday or a discount notification. Associate Professor in the School of Fashion and Textiles at RMIT University and study co-author Carol Tan said this behaviour was known as "strategic spontaneity". "You think it's impulsive, but it's actually planned," she said. "So what people do is they save the items, they have a wish list, and then they monitor their sales and wait for payday. "It could be sitting in their cart for a week or a month, and then a spur-of-the-moment decision is when they actually make the purchase and it happens in minutes." Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au The fast and ultra-fast fashion gap While fast fashion has been around for some time, platforms such as Shein and Temu differ in their production and distribution methods. Traditional fast-fashion brands release a new collection every two to four weeks that can range from hundreds to thousands of styles and sell primarily through physical stores. Ultra-fast fashion stores produce 2,000 to 10,000 new styles daily and use digital-only, mobile app-dominant sales models. Dr Tan said the rise of ultra-fast fashion has pushed some fast-fashion brands to change their strategy. "They are trying to not compete with the Sheins of the world and they are trying to go a bit more upmarket. So they sell better-quality stuff and they have like $400 jackets," she said. Outside of the growing price gap between fast fashion and ultra-fashion fashion, Dr Tan said these sites often sold items you could not buy in brick-and-mortar stores. Despite participants expressing concerns about the environmental and ethical impacts of ultra-fast fashion brands, many still continued to purchase on Shein or Temu. According to the latest figures from the Australia Institute, on average Australians purchase 56 items of clothing a year. It also reports more than 200,000 tonnes of clothing end up in Australian landfills each year. The study found participants were more influenced by social and economic drivers than long-term ethical concerns. I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out. I try to buy sustainable brands, but they are so expensive. Shein is just there and it's easy. If the big brands are allowed to sell it, then it can't be all my fault for buying it. I feel bad sometimes, but one small top isn't going to destroy the ocean. The study also found buyers would draw on explanations such as reduced feelings of personal responsibility, affordability constraints, limited access to sustainable alternatives and the belief that the individual purchases had little impact. In some countries, different taxes have been introduced to deter buyers from ultra-fast fashion brands. France has banned advertising from ultra-fast fashion businesses and introduced a fee that will rise to €10 ($16) per item by 2030. New Zealand has a levy of NZ$2.21 ($1.80) per package.

events.title: Charity provides school lunches for kids as food insecurity rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts National school lunch program launched in Moe aims to tackle food insecurity Victoria and Brandon are big fans of the Spoonfull program. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) A new universal school meals program launched in Moe offers healthy lunches to primary school children. The program aims to tackle food insecurity as well as improving student wellbeing and learning outcomes. The charity Eat Up hopes to roll out the program across Australia to schools in need. It is lunchtime at Elizabeth Street Primary School at Moe in Victoria's east. On today's menu, a chicken pasta bake is the hot option, and tuna and salad rolls are on offer for others. The children queuing up are told that the more they can stack on their plates, the better. "I love the food, it's amazing," student Victoria says. "My favourite has been the lasagne and butter chicken, and I really like the wraps they make. "They give options to us that if we don't like a food, then we can just try it and I just love how they do that." A team of volunteers helps to prepare the students' lunches. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The lunches are part of a program that aims to tackle child hunger and improve student wellbeing across the country. The charity Eat Up has launched its pilot program Spoonfull at the school, a universal meal program that provides every student at participating schools with a healthy lunch, every day. Ian Frost and Carol O'Reilly say they have seen a huge improvement since the program was introduced. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The program was officially launched at Elizabeth Street Primary School in its purpose-built Hearts and Hands Learning Kitchen, after some strong lobbying by the school's wellbeing officer Carol O'Reilly. "I could see a need. I've been at this school for 17 years and I noticed running [the school's] breakfast club that kids are coming in without sandwiches," Ms O'Reilly said. "Now I know they're going out for recess with a full belly." She said learning outcomes and student welfare had improved greatly since the introduction of the program. "The kids are smiling. You can see them outside, they're playing and they're just dying to know what's for lunch." Students are offered a variety of healthy foods, including a hot lunch. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) School principal Ian Frost said the school lunch program had a positive impact on what students eat and had led to improved wellbeing and academic performance. Eat Up has been running for 15 years, delivering more than 6 million free on-demand school lunches to children experiencing food insecurity. Charity founder Lyndon Galea said the Spoonfull program built upon that business model to offer something more sustainable for schools to support students long-term. "This is different to our core model, [where] we have on-demand lunches, in terms of the cheese sandwiches, yoghurts and recess snacks," Mr Galea said. "We've learnt of certain schools where there's perhaps a higher number of kids arriving without food from home or where the socio-economic need bites even harder," he said. Lyndon Galea founded Eat Up 15 years ago. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) At Elizabeth Street Primary School, Spoonfull helped fund upgrades to the school kitchen to have commercial fridges and ovens, with hopes of also installing a dishwasher. Loophole closed after rare private prosecution shuts Hepburn council Wilsons Prom's Sealers Cove track reopens after five years 'Grand old dame' mountain chalet to reopen after more than 20 years Warner Bros killed Coyote vs. Acme, but now it's back According to Australian Bureau of Statistics data from 2023, about 16 to 22 per cent of Australian children experience food insecurity. Single-parent households and low-income families were at the highest risk. As the cost of living continues to affect families, so too has the growth in food insecurity. "Families who are already in a difficult spot are needing help more often and then a lot of families who have historically been just above that level of need and needing support are accessing food support for the very first time," Mr Galea said. Through support from Spoonfull, the school was able to make key upgrades to its kitchen. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) Eat Up hopes to have enough support to roll out similar pilots in two additional schools. "I think it would be phenomenal for Australia and something our country can really take a big step forward [in]," Mr Galea said. Elizabeth Street Primary School student Victoria agreed and said she thought all schools could benefit from the program.

events.title: US, China open high-level talks ahead of Trump-Xi summit
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Scott Bessent and He Lifeng meet in New York for US-China talks ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting later this week. Top economic officials from China and the United States have begun talks in New York City aimed at clearing the way for possible agreements on trade, artificial intelligence and critical minerals ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng began talks at JPMorgan Chase’s Manhattan headquarters on Sunday morning, with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer also taking part. list 1 of 4 China faces oil challenge as prices soar and supply options narrow list 2 of 4 Taiwan flexes military capabilities ahead of Trump-Xi talks list 3 of 4 Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’ with new ‘AI czar’ list 4 of 4 Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise? The talks come four days before Trump is due to host Xi at the White House, with both sides looking to ease tensions between the world’s two largest economies. “I’m looking forward to having focused, fulsome and constructive talks today that will set the stage for our leaders’ meeting,” Bessent told reporters as he arrived. At the top of the agenda is a fragile US-China trade truce due to expire on November 10. The agreement, reached in Busan, South Korea, last November, capped US tariffs on Chinese goods at about 20 percent after a tit-for-tat trade fight briefly pushed tariffs into the triple digits. Washington is also pressuring Beijing over its supply of rare-earth magnets and other critical minerals, crucial to industries ranging from cars to advanced semiconductors. China promised to restore the flow of critical minerals under last year’s truce, but a senior US official said on Friday that Beijing’s performance had “not been up to par”. Artificial intelligence (AI) is also expected to feature prominently, adding a relatively new issue to negotiations long dominated by trade. Bessent has said the countries could discuss AI “guardrails” aimed at addressing shared risks, including preventing powerful models from falling into the hands of malign non-state actors. The talks are expected to cover both open- and closed-weight AI models. Chinese open-weight models have increasingly attracted US companies, in part because they can be cheaper than closed systems developed by US firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic. “The United States remains the leader in AI,” Bessent said. “And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems.” Another potential point of friction is Iran. China remains one of Tehran’s most important economic partners and buys much of its oil, making Beijing an important target of Washington’s efforts to increase economic pressure on Iran as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its seventh month. Despite the packed agenda, analysts are not expecting a sweeping breakthrough. “I think there will be some show of deliverables because of the fact that it’s a presidential summit coming, but I don’t feel like we’re on the verge of some sort of breakthrough,” Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence, told Reuters. “I think status quo is probably both sides’ general best expectation.” Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell similarly said the immediate goal may simply be keeping tensions contained. “One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year,” Campbell said. Sunday’s negotiations are part of a series of meetings between Bessent, He and Greer over the past 16 months aimed at hammering out areas of agreement before Trump and Xi meet face to face.

events.title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget
events.summary: Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue. Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10. As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”. Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson , the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique. “People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.” She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures , saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget. The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures. She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home. “We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end. “And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister. “I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation. She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco. Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.” With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties. She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister. “It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

events.title: France’s Macron and Canada’s Carney announce plans to build stronger ties
events.summary: Announcement comes as Canada seeks a closer relationship with the EU amid a trade war with the US. Canada and France will pursue cooperation on energy, defence, space and other sectors, in what their leaders say is a reflection of shared values between the two countries. The announcement was made on Sunday during a joint media conference by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron on the island archipelago of Saint Pierre and Miquelon in the North Atlantic. list 1 of 3 Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership? list 2 of 3 Trump says deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland list 3 of 3 Canadians warm to EU ‘associate membership’ proposal The French territory is only about 25km (15.5 miles) from Newfoundland in Canada. Macron said it is a reflection of the historic closeness between the two countries, who “see the present from the same angle”. Parts of Canada were once French colonies and French is still one of Canada’s two official languages, along with English. “We both believe in democracy, in the rule of law, in the respect of international law, in the respect of free and fair commerce and trade,” Macron said alongside Carney. “That is why we support this future alliance, that you named as an associate member of the EU.” Carney said both countries see eye to eye on protecting sovereignty, and that this meant going beyond “being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves” to being able to secure access to AI, space, semiconductors, critical minerals and clean energy. Carney said the time had come to strengthen bonds between Canada, France and the European Union based on their “shared values”. The remarks came as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States amid the escalating trade dispute between the neighbours and instead move closer to the EU. Carney has said Canada seeks a “unique alliance” with the economic and political bloc, which would fall short of being a full member state. Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member.” Canadian and European leaders have openly said they want to forge closer bonds to distance themselves from the United States and the political direction it seems to be going. “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” Carney said in a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.” United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada and make it the “51st state”. He has also called for Greenland to be taken away from Denmark and made a part of the US. But this week, he said he was happy with an agreement that he claimed would give Washington “permanent control” over the island, which largely enjoys self-rule but is still a part of Denmark. Both Greenland and Denmark said after the agreement was announced that any deal with the US would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty. Trump has called Ottawa’s attempt to move closer to the EU “laughable” and said he would have to study exactly what membership would mean. If it did not satisfy him, Trump said it could be seen as a “hostile act”. “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs,” Trump said. He also suggested that the US could stop trading with Europe “on many things”. Canada and the US have been locked in a trade war after failing to reach an agreement. The Trump administration imposed up to 50 percent tariffs on nearly $20bn worth of Canadian products, including machinery, textiles and even hockey sticks. Canada imposed retaliatory measures and the impasse continues.

events.title: Trump to meet with Zelensky as Russia-Ukraine attacks intensify
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a phone call with President Trump on Sunday that the two will meet this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Why it matters: The meeting comes as the White House works to broker an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to take reciprocal steps to deescalate and resume negotiations — and as fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent days. Zelensky's chief negotiator and the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov, told Axios he's been working with White House envoys in recent days to organize the meeting, which is expected to happen Tuesday. Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months. What he's saying: "An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelensky wrote on X. Zelensky said Ukraine is ready "to take really serious steps" to reach a deescalation deal with Russia. Behind the scenes: A source familiar with the call said Trump repeatedly asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The strikes are driving up global diesel prices. "The word diesel came up many times during the call," the source said. The intrigue: Earlier this week the Kyiv Independent reported that the Ukrainian government was "growing increasingly frustrated" with White House envoy Steve Witkoff. The story came out several days after Witkoff and Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time since the war began. Umerov told Axios the story was false. "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," he said. He added that he's been working with Witkoff and Kushner on a daily basis over the last year. "Our main focus is on finding solutions for ending the war and gaining security guarantees and prosperity to Ukrainian people," he added. Umerov said the negotiations are under close public and media scrutiny and therefore "it comes with criticism." "Nevertheless, we need to stay focused. Steve has done a great job with us. We do not waste time and stay focused on finding solutions," he said. State of play: Umerov said significant progress has been made in the talks. "In particular, the number of stumbling blocks reduced from dozens to essentially one or two key issues that remain subject to negotiations," he said. "The trend is positive. The U.S. is super focused on the issue of stopping the war in Ukraine. The U.S. understands the situation on the battlefield, and signals to everyone that this terrible war should end," Umerov said. Yes, but: Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have escalated in recent days, with both sides conducting more long-range attacks. On Sunday, Ukraine launched a missile attack on Moscow and hit an oil refinery. Russia has been launching missiles at Kyiv and other major cities almost every day in recent weeks. While Russia has signaled willingness to consider steps to deescalate ahead of winter — and a resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine — there has been little progress towards an actual deal.

events.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says AI CEOs have 'ulterior reasons' for warning about doomsday
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI leaders are being disingenuous in their calls for more regulation. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI leaders are being disingenuous when calling for a slowdown. Huang said current regulations are enough to ensure the tech remains safe and profitable. Huang's comments echo those of President Donald Trump. Don't let the black leather jacket fool you, Jensen Huang isn't a doomer. Nvidia's CEO said as much in an interview with CBS News aired on Sunday. He accused the leaders of the frontier AI labs of being disingenuous in their warnings that, without more AI oversight, the products they are building could harm humanity in myriad forms. "Go and read between the lines," Huang said, referring to AI leaders calling for government regulation of the industry . "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have." "They must be doing it for ulterior reasons," he added. Huang said he didn't know exactly what those ulterior reasons are, but that scaring people about the tech is "irresponsible" and "unnecessary." Huang's comments on Sunday echo those of President Donald Trump, who said on Saturday that new regulations aren't needed to ensure the tech remains safe. "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the president said on Truth Social, his social media platform. Michael Kratsios , the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, has also rejected the idea that tech companies need government intervention to ensure the safety of their AI models. In a Fox News interview on Sunday, he said the AI labs could just go ahead and "just stop" if they think their products are dangerous. Last week, a chorus of leading AI CEOs said AI development should be slowed down until adequate risk-prevention measures could be put in place. In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-pronged plan that would, in his view, strengthen safeguards to ensure AI remains under the control of human engineers. One of those prongs included calls for the US government, "for antitrust reasons," to regulate frontier AI labs. Amodei's essay was signal-boosted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Huang has emerged as a prominent anti-regulation voice, together with Trump and David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech. In the CBS interview, Huang reiterated previous concerns that a slowdown among US labs would cede ground to China in the global AI race, and that AI labs don't need government help to implement a slowdown. "We don't need more regulations," Huang said. "We need to apply the current regulations we have." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hacking this BYD was too easy. It didn't even have a password
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts We got a cybersecurity expert to hack this BYD. It was too easy On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister. But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control; a hacker has access to the car. As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work. With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness. The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the past two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert who specialises in cars. His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer. "It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says. Modern connected cars, particularly EVs and hybrids, are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before. In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China. With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands. EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers because they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities. To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD. Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity. "The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says. This lack of a password allowed Hreszczuk to access the car's digital arteries. From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which controlled different functions in the car. After two weeks, Hreszczuk was ready. Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what can be done with remote access to a vehicle. First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen. Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off. The combination is unsettling and highly distracting. Adding to the distraction, Hreszczuk has the speaker telling me repeatedly: "For safety, use low beam." Fortunately, I was only travelling 30 kilometres per hour and the road was pretty straight. Then, Hreszczuk kills the lights altogether. Hreszczuk says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected. But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road. While sabotage is one worry, the concern most often cited is surveillance due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV. Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs, even those made with Chinese components, from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations. China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential. In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices. But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV. Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Hreszczuk hacked. Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned". ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Hreszczuk is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access. We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mother a call to talk her through some internet banking. As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Hreszczuk has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress. "How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab. At that point Hreszczuk can hear everything. When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking. "I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.

events.title: Is the AI industry really ready to slow down?
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt We’re seeing a big debate over AI safety and a potential slowdown, as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a plan to “pace the frontier,” while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly echoed President Donald Trump’s claims that the AI backlash is a hoax and regulation is unnecessary. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed whether executives like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are serious about wanting to slow down. While I was surprised at how many industry leaders seemed to throw their support behind Amodei’s plan, Sean noted that the plan seemed short on details. And when Kristen asked whether a combination of existing regulation and the workings of the free market could provide enough safeguards on their own, Sean replied, “We have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.” Plus, he argued, “There does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony Ha: Sean, what do you think? Are we actually going to”‘pace the frontier”? Sean O’Kane: That sounds, for some reason, like something from “Point Break.” It’s just a very California statement, like, “We’re gonna pace the frontier, bruh.” I don’t know. I said on this show last week , I didn’t think we were headed for a slowdown of any kind, in large part because I don’t think these companies are structured in a way where that works. So this was a pretty immediate flip of what I said a week ago, to hear this from Dario at Anthropic and Sam at OpenAI and even Elon Musk to a certain degree — and we can get into whether we believe that or not. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down. Anthony, I know you read this stuff pretty closely last weekend as it was all popping off, so I’m curious if you’re maybe more generous than I am, as far as understanding what it is they’re trying to say here. Anthony: I mean, I also have questions. What really stood out to me is the fact that so many people in the industry seemed to coalesce around this fairly quickly. Even before Amodei published his blog post, I was seeing other people post some version of this [plan,] just in the days leading up to it. My understanding is, these suggestions that have come out of the AI safety community; these are things that have been percolating for a while. They’re not just things that [Amodei] thought up on his own. But it just seemed like a lot of people were kind of ready to embrace this and in some ways, [it’s] encouraging to see that there’s a consensus. But it also makes me a little skeptical that this would represent genuine, major steps towards a slowdown. Kirsten Korosec: First of all, consensus can be a good thing. Also, it can be the beginnings of forming a cartel. And so, let’s be clear [about] who we’re talking about here. We’re talking about frontier AI labs. and that’s specific and important. You did say a minute ago that the details aren’t really clear, but we do know that the general idea here is that independent third party evaluators would come in that would work inside [companies] like Anthropic or OpenAI and monitor AI safety practices and incidents. But there is a lot of vagueness around that. Then there’s another proposal to have major AI companies in democratic countries coordinate on safety standards and limits. And then this international coordination piece. So those are the general ideas around this. I’ll also add that there’s been very considerable pushback from very specific people. And surprisingly, some people I didn’t think would push back on this. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. I don’t know what either of you think of […] some of his comments and the call he took from President Trump on-stage [at the All-In Summit] Sean: I think Jensen understands that, to a certain extent, he is seen as the adult in the room here. Which is interesting, because that’s a dynamic that I think has changed.

events.title: My 13-year-old refused to share his location with me. I was annoyed — until I realized he had a point.
events.summary: The author (not pictured) didn't think she was a helicopter mom until her son pushed back on tracking. Carol Yepes/Getty Images I let my 13-year-old spend time with friends without constant supervision. When I asked to track his location, he argued that he'd earned my trust. I stopped routinely tracking him and now rely mostly on communication. I don't think of myself as an overprotective parent . I began letting my kids stay home alone for short stints when they were around 10. I let them wander our neighborhood alone starting when they were 11 or 12. I don't heavily monitor their social lives or phone usage, nor do I check their grades constantly or make them give me access to their Google Classroom to monitor their schoolwork. But I don't do things the same way that my generation's parents did things. I'm Generation X , and in my generation, there were no "playdates." Parents didn't track your grades, and they definitely didn't track your location. You'd be walking around the neighborhood alone at 6 or 7 years old, often for hours. Usually your parents had no idea where you were. The hope was that you'd come home sometime before dark. I didn't realize I was a helicopter parent When my youngest son turned 13, he started going out with friends on his own. Sometimes he'd take a friend's school bus home with them, and hang out for a few hours. Other times, he'd walk over to a friend's house, and then walk around town. I supported this — it reminded me of the freedom I experienced as a teenager and I know how important that was for my own development. My son is super responsible, and doesn't make social plans without letting me know. That's why I didn't think it would be such a big deal when I asked him to share his location with me on his phone. The author asked her teenage son to track his location. Courtesy of the author I didn't think of tracking as an invasion of my son's privacy. It just felt normal, the same way that I can see his grades as they come in on the school portal if I choose to. Or the way that I ask my son to text me about his social plans as they unfold, rather than just sending him out and expecting him to come back by nightfall. But my son was adamant about me not tracking his location . My first reaction was, "I'm giving you freedom to do whatever you want, so I should be able to see where you are!" But as he made his case to me — that he is responsible and will update me, but doesn't like the idea of me tracking his every movement — I totally saw his point. It's one thing to tell your parents what you're doing, and when you're coming home, but do parents really need to monitor every step a child takes? I understand the idea of knowing a child's location so that you might be able to find them if you don't end up hearing from them. But honestly, if something awful were to happen, there's no way to be sure they'd still have their phone on them, or that tracking them would be able to protect them in any significant way. Plus, I saw my son's point. I put my own teenage self in his position. If my parents had some way to track every move I made back in the day, I definitely would have felt resentful. It made me reflect on modern parenting After this happened, I realized that — without fully noticing it — I'd adopted so many overbearing aspects of modern parenting. I have a college student, and I see parents freaking out when they find out they can no longer monitor their kids' grades, and that kids (not parents) have to email the financial aid and school housing departments to take care of school business. The author says the experience made her reflect on modern parenting. Courtesy of the author Our kids are eventually going to be grown-ups, and if we don't begin to loosen our grips on them, I fear that they are going to go into adulthood completely ill-equipped to handle anything on their own. I know this world is dangerous, and knowing where your child is located may make you feel more confident as you let them venture out into the world. But you also have to consider your child's mental health and development and what it might mean for them to feel as though you are tracking every move they make. Kids need to feel like their lives are their own and that the world is a place they can explore without constant scrutiny. We came up with a compromise that worked for both of us Despite all this, I realized that certain aspects of modern parenthood and things like GPS tracking technology can be helpful. So my son and I came up with a compromise. For the most part, I don't ask him to share his location with me, but I expect him to keep me updated about his plans, and text me if he needs to be picked up or if any other issues emerge while he's out. But there are times when we end up using his phone's tracking feature, such as when he shares the location of where he needs to be picked up or when he's exploring an area that he's less familiar with. This balance has made sense for our family because it's based on open communication, deep listening, and giving my son as much freedom as possible so that he can mature into a strong, resilient, and independent young adult. events.title: Vocci’s ring adds a new form factor to meeting note-taking
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt There is no dearth of different forms of hardware for meeting note-taking , including pendants, pins, and credit-card-styled devices. That hasn’t stopped Vocci from releasing a new device for the same use case in a ring form factor, which is convenient but could create some privacy issues. The ring form factor is one of the easiest for anyone who wants to just press a button and have the device start recording. Pebble’s new Index 01 Ring, which I am testing right now, lets you hold the button and take a note or a reminder. Stream Ring, made by Sandbar, works similarly with a control pad on the top. Vocci’s ring takes a different path, with meeting note-taking as a central function. The ring has a button, which you can double-tap to start recording and double-tap again to stop. You can tap and hold the button to ask Vocci AI questions, but that only works when you have the app open. There is an indicator light and a haptic motor for recording feedback. The ring is lightweight at under 6 grams and uses titanium material on the inner and outer surfaces — likely a coating. The company claims that the Vocci ring can record notes for 8 hours on a single charge. The device comes with a chunky plastic case, which can charge the ring up to three times. The device captures meetings very well. I have had conversations spanning more than an hour in loud cafes, and the ring managed to convert most of the chat into accurate transcripts. However, this method of note-taking is not great if you want to take short notes. The software is the disappointing part of the Vocci ring. The app itself is a bit confusing. Whenever I took shorter notes, I saw AI-generated insights that were longer than the notes themselves. Each recording has Chat, which is the main transcript; Highlights, which are short snippets you can capture by pressing the button while recording a conversation; and Notes, which is a summary and insight of the whole conversation. In the app, there is a tab called Base where you can find transcripts, recordings, and anything you generate from them, and I found that redundant. I didn’t find a way to directly initiate a chat with AI for session transcripts. Voice-enabled rings are a great form factor for taking short notes or reminders. The app doesn’t have direct integration with reminder apps, which is a bummer. The feature rollout for its software is also slow. The company informed me that users can use Vocci’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to other assistants, but the option to do that didn’t appear until a few weeks ago in the app. Other meeting notetakers are building their platforms to allow users to automate insights and workflow through AI, and at the moment, Vocci’s platform is not fully built out for that. There are some privacy concerns with this device because of its form factor. Vocci’s ring looks like a regular piece of jewellery until someone notices the button on it. The ring has a recording indicator, but it faces the user. It’s best practice to let someone know that you are recording a conversation, and it’s also required by law in some countries and regions. But with this kind of device, some micreants can easily choose not to disclose that information and record the conversation without anyone noticing. The company said it encourages people to disclose that they are recording, but that may not be enough. At $249, the ring is pricey compared to other notetakers like Plaud or Pocket , and that is due to the device’s lightweight form factor. The ring is for someone who doesn’t want to stick a gadget on the back of their phone, wear a wristband, or wear a pendant. On the hardware layer, a lot of these devices are combinations of some microphones, a battery, and a connection to the phone. We will likely see more variety in hardware meeting note-takers in the coming years, until users pick the specific formats that work for them. events.title: Man Utd salvage Fulham draw as pressure mounts on Carrick
events.summary: Matheus Cunha strikes late as Manchester United seal a 1-1 draw at Fulham, but pressure mounts on manager Michael Carrick. Manchester United rescued a 1-1 draw against Fulham thanks to Matheus Cunha’s late equaliser on Sunday, but the pressure is mounting on boss Michael Carrick after their latest lacklustre display. Carrick’s football side were in dire need of a victory at Craven Cottage, but instead left grateful for a point. list 1 of 4 India’s Mandhana breaks T20 record in Asian Games cricket semifinal win list 2 of 4 Asian Games: Opening ceremony offers respite amid mounting complaints list 3 of 4 Asian Games: Emotions run high as Iran win bronze in men’s basketball list 4 of 4 Eala and Pathirage headline top athletes to watch at the 2026 Asian Games United fell behind in the second half to a farcical own goal from Lisandro Martinez, who diverted the ball into his own net after Senne Lammens had saved Calvin Bassey’s shot. Although Cunha’s last-gasp leveller spared United from a third successive defeat, there was little reason for celebration for Carrick and his beleaguered team. United have just one win in five Premier League matches and already trail leaders Manchester City by 10 points. They have lost three of their first seven games in all competitions this season and head into the international break with Carrick under intense scrutiny. Carrick has insisted that he does not care about his future at Old Trafford. But after successive gut-punch defeats against Manchester City and Brighton, this was another setback to his reeling regime. Shell-shocked by Erling Haaland’s winner for City in last weekend’s derby – which the referees’ governing body later admitted should have been disallowed – United blew a 2-0 lead against Brighton in the League Cup third round on Wednesday. Barely escaping with a draw against second-from-bottom Fulham was another indignity in a season already full of forgettable moments for United. Expected to at least match last season’s third-place finish, United have gone backwards since Carrick was appointed as manager on a permanent basis following his successful interim spell. United return to action with a home game against bottom-of-the-table Tottenham on October 10, with Carrick and Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi both desperate for a win that would turn the tide. Foreshadowing their afternoon of struggle, United were fortunate not to fall behind in the opening moments when Fulham forward Gonzalo Garcia dragged his shot wide from a dangerous position. That narrow escape triggered a response from United as Bruno Fernandes picked out Martinez for a stinging strike from the edge of the penalty area, forcing Bernd Leno to make a superb save. United went close again when Cunha pulled his pass back to Fernandes, whose fierce strike cannoned off the post. But United were jittery at the back, and Josh King’s half-volley forced a good save from Lammens before the goalkeeper denied Sander Berge with another smart stop. Oscar Bobb should have beaten Lammens moments later, but he was off target with a golden opportunity to break the deadlock. With United far too open, Fulham poured forward in waves in the closing minutes of the first half. Lammens had to claw away another blast from King, then raced off his line to frustrate Alex Iwobi as the pressure mounted. United’s lack of drive and cutting edge, combined with some shambolic defending, provided a fatal cocktail that led to Fulham’s opener. After Cunha carelessly conceded possession deep inside United’s half, Carrick’s men were slow to react as Bassey unloaded a powerful strike that was palmed out by Lammens. Martinez tried to clear the ball, but his bizarrely mistimed swipe directed it back into his own net via a deflection off the despairing Lammens. Leno kept out Bryan Mbeumo’s curler and plunged to his left to save Cunha’s low drive as United tried desperately to salvage a point. United’s late flurry brought an equaliser in the 89th minute. Cunha tried his luck from distance, and his shot took a wicked deflection off David Affengruber. For once, Carrick’s luck was in.

events.title: U.S. economy hits pivotal milestone: Spending on data centers and other information-processing hardware now exceeds housing investment
events.summary: Two decades after the housing boom reshaped, then tanked, the U.S. economy, the AI boom is similarly transforming the drivers of growth. Hyperscalers have poured so much money into building as much AI infrastructure as possible—and as quickly as possible—that investment from a handful of companies is expected to reach $1 trillion a year soon. Meanwhile, the housing market has been largely frozen since the COVID-era boom ended in 2022, when the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive rate-hiking campaign to rein in inflation. “We’re seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers,” Adam Shapiro, vice president at the San Francisco Fed, posted on LinkedIn recently. He pointed out that inflation-adjusted spending on information processing equipment, which includes data centers and computer hardware, now exceeds residential investment. According to data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, real private residential fixed investment was $748 billion in the second quarter, down 18% from an early 2021 peak. During that same span, spending on information processing equipment has soared 51% to $752 billion. “The AI investment boom is massive,” Shapiro added. He also noted that residential investment is more sensitive to borrowing costs, which have gone up alongside Treasury yields. The benchmark 30-year mortgage rate is nearly 7% as the 10-year bond yield has hit the highest level since 2007. By contrast, AI investment has been less sensitive to interest rates, even as hyperscalers have started issuing more debt to supplement drawdowns of their cash piles. Google parent Alphabet , for example, even reported negative cash flow earlier this year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also highlighted the eagerness with which AI companies are offering debt—no matter the cost of borrowing. “We are also seeing big corporate issuance. And a lot of that corporate issuance, I would say, is almost yield-agnostic, because the build-out for AI, the returns on that, the companies believe they’re going to be so high. They don’t really care what they’re paying,” he said recently. The onslaught of AI spending is expected to keep ramping up. S&P Global estimated last month that capital expenditures from Alphabet, Amazon , Microsoft , Meta , Oracle , and SpaceX will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. The ratings firm added that the industry’s capex is growing faster than revenue, warning that the aggressive build-out could lead to overcapacity if future demand doesn’t pan out as expected. S&P sees 2028 as an inflection point, with revenue accelerating and capex flattening. Until then, however, operating cash flow from the six hyperscalers will collectively be negative in 2026 and 2027, it added. The breakneck speed of AI development has also generated immense political backlash that’s rippling through the midterm election season. A new NBC News poll found that 64% of registered voters said they’d be less likely to support a candidate who’s in favor of building a data center in their community. AI has also fed into the cost-of-living crisis as consumers grapple with higher electricity bills and prices for new smartphones and PCs. That’s added to angst with home prices remaining out of reach for many Americans. While increased housing supply would ease pressure on prices, availability has been limited. The supply of existing homes has been constrained by the “lock-in” effect of homeowners with low mortgage rates reluctant to give them up amid today’s high rates. And new construction has been weak as high rates weigh on demand while building costs grow. Housing starts fell 2.6% in August to an annualized pace of 1.275 million, led by a drop in multifamily projects. While single-family homes rose, permits fell, signaling muted activity in the future. Meanwhile, the National Association of Home Builders reported builder sentiment fell to its lowest level in a year. “The big picture remains that elevated and rising borrowing costs are holding developers back, supporting our view that the downward trend in housing starts has further to run,” Capital Economics said in a recent note. events.title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through? That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll. ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end. “The younger generation is increasingly going short form, vertical feed only (especially the 18 year olds we’ve spoken to!), and this poses challenges for any kind of media that requires depth,” Utsav Gupta, ScrollEd’s co-founder, told TechCrunch in an email. “We want to meet them where they are…We just have to be deliberate about how we use it and choose not to maximize engagement on the platform.” “A short video can make you curious; following that curiosity can mean searching for another explanation or leaving the app,” Gupta continued. “We wanted going deeper to be as easy as moving to the next video.” Gupta bootstrapped ScrollEd this year alongside his co-founder and wife Rebecca Neff after the two both noticed feeling dissatisfied after doomscrolling before bed. Both are students — Gupta studies AI and human purpose at Stanford, and Neff studies computer science at the University of Pennsylvania. The startup is targeting educational institutions, corporate training programs, and individuals who “just want something better to scroll on,” according to Gupta. The company will launch its consumer business at Disrupt. (“We’re hoping to ‘disrupt’ social media and short form!” Gupta joked.) ScrollEd is following a freemium model, combining a free consumer feed with a paid ScrollEd Pro subscription and annual institutional licenses. Institutions pay to deliver educational material through the platform, in exchange for reports about engagement, lesson progress, and other data. In the coming months, ScrollEd intends to focus on its consumer launch, building its lesson library and source-checking workflow, and developing pilots for institutions. The startup is also building infrastructure that will one day allow educators to assess individual learners and adapt to their needs. “The ambition is a social network that’s better for you,” Gupta said. events.title: Trump's tech advisor has advice for AI companies worried they're building unsafe models: 'Just stop'
events.summary: Michael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Tech leaders say the pace of AI development needs to slow down, and asked the government to step in. Trump's technology advisor, however, says companies don't need the government's permission to do so. The Trump administration has broadly supported expanding and accelerating AI infrastructure. There's a simple solution for AI companies that feel like their models are developing at a frightening speed: Hit the brakes. That's the advice Michael Kratsios , the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, gave during an interview with Fox News Sunday. "It's very interesting that they talk about these issues, about how scared they are about potentially where the future is, and maybe they want to do a pause," Kratsios said. "Our position is, if you do believe that you're developing a technology that is unsafe or you don't want it out into the world, you can just stop it." He added, "You don't need someone to force you to do that." Kratsios pushed back against the notion that the US government needs to take explicit action for tech companies to take a breather. "They just need to slow down if they feel that they need to do so," Kratsios said. "I think the key thing to always remember is the US government has lots of tools in its toolkit to deal with these issues when they come up, and we've used them in the past." Ever since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, tech companies across the globe have become locked in a race to develop the most capable model. Doing so could mean dominating the market and securing steady profits, a huge win for whichever company comes out on top. OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are among the industry leaders. Many Americans have expressed concerns that those tech companies are moving too fast and, in doing so, putting public safety at risk. A Pew Research Center survey published in August said over half of the respondents were more concerned than excited about using AI more in their daily lives. Potential job loss was among the top concerns associated with AI. Critics have also pointed toward privacy and cybersecurity risks. In July, OpenAI agents breached its training parameters and hacked Hugging Face , another AI company. This month, a cybersecurity startup used Anthropic's Claude to hack OpenAI's codebase . On Friday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring. AI leaders themselves have long expressed concern about the products they are raising hundreds of billions of dollars to build. In a blog post earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the Hugging Face breach convinced him that the industry needs to take its foot off the pedal. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," Amodei wrote. He suggested placing independent safety monitors inside the frontier AI labs and called for more robust government regulation. The blog post earned support from his industry peers, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis. President Donald Trump , who has broadly supported expanding and accelerating AI development in the US, said on Saturday that his administration would not do anything that could "stifle" AI's progress. He also announced a new AI Force to coordinate responses when AI goes off the rails. The Trump administration supported the $500 billion Stargate Project , an initiative to expand AI infrastructure nationwide, and he signed an executive order to accelerate federal permitting for data center construction. He will host China's leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington, D.C., this week to discuss AI and trade. Kratsios told Fox News Sunday that it's critical to have conversations about AI with China. "The key thing that we want to talk to him about is avoiding shared risks, and that's something that I think we can have a fruitful conversation on," Kratsios said. events.title: Trump tariffs hit Canada’s dairy farmers as US sales stall
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections A 50 percent tariff has disrupted dairy exports, leaving Canadian farmers with milk that cannot be redirected overnight. Reporting from the Fraser Valley in British Columbia Abbotsford, British Columbia – Every second day, 28,000 litres of raw milk leave Casey Pruim’s farm in Abbotsford in western Canada, entering a distribution system built on the assumption that the milk and the products made from it will have somewhere to go. While most is consumed in Canada, some had been sold across the border to the United States. Those sales have largely come to a standstill since US President Donald Trump’s 50 percent tariff on $20bn in Canadian goods, including dairy products, came into effect on August 22. Pruim, who is also chair of the British Columbia Dairy Association representing about 400 dairy farmers across the province, told Al Jazeera that Canadian farmers do not individually decide which products are exported. Instead, producers such as Pruim – whose farm has 330 cows milked three times a day – sell into the provincial milk-marketing system, which distributes milk to processors according to demand, including for products exported to the US. If a processor loses US demand, it may require less milk, with the impact then spread across the provincial pool. Dylan Kruger, director of public affairs at BC Dairy, told Al Jazeera “there is still considerable uncertainty around the impact of the US tariffs”. He said it was too early to know how the industry would be impacted or whether milk no longer sold to the US could be sold elsewhere, mitigating financial losses. But the tariffs and wider trade tensions have already introduced uncertainty and instability for businesses. “If the processor who’s exporting some of his product to the United States can no longer sell into that market because he’s now priced out of the market with a 50 percent tariff, that’s how it would impact the dairy farm,” Pruim said. Pruim said if processor demand is squeezed, farmers would be forced to dump the milk. In the worst-case scenario, the herd has to be cut. “Cows aren’t like a tap; you can’t just turn them on or off,” he said. His warning captures dairy’s particular vulnerability in a tariff war: Milk is highly perishable, collected on a tight schedule and dependent on processors whose demand can change much faster than farmers can adjust production. “These tariffs are completely unwarranted,” David Wiens, president of the Dairy Farmers of Canada, told Canada’s CBC News, adding that they would affect “the supply chain, not only in Canada but in the US as well”. Dairy trade between Canada and the US has largely operated under a free trade agreement between the US, Mexico and Canada, known as CUSMA in Canada. Canada manages the supply of dairy, poultry and eggs through a national agricultural policy known as supply management. The system uses production quotas and import controls, including tariffs, to provide farmers with more stable and predictable prices while maintaining domestic supply. Critics describe the system as protectionist and as a government-backed cartel. Washington argues that Canada’s supply-management system restricts US dairy exports. Trump posted on Truth Social that “Canada had been ripping off the United States of America for years” and accused it of imposing “ridiculously high tariffs” that made life impossible for US farmers. Canadian producers reject that argument, saying the existing trade agreement already gives US imports substantial tariff-free access that is not fully utilised. Canada’s dairy trade deficit with the US has grown significantly since CUSMA came into force on July 1, 2020, according to the Dairy Processors Association of Canada. In 2020, Canada exported 241.3 million Canadian dollars ($173m) in dairy products to the US and imported 647.4 million Canadian dollars ($462.7m) worth of dairy and dairy products. In 2025, Canadian dairy exports had risen to 308.7 million Canadian dollars ($220.7m) while dairy imports from the US had more than doubled to 1.355 billion Canadian dollars ($968.5m), accounting for 13.8 percent of total value of US dairy exports, according to the association. Bryan Yu, chief economist at Central 1 credit union, said the immediate shock of losing a major market could be difficult for Canadian producers to absorb because replacement buyers cannot be found quickly. “There is going to be pain in the near term for a lot of our producers,” Yu told Al Jazeera. “You really can’t quickly adjust to a 50 percent tariff, because it’s uncharted waters for a lot of industries … and ultimately it shuts [Canadian producers] out, because a lot of them don’t have the margins that they can play with,” he said. Yu said Canadian consumers might absorb some of the additional supply while exporters search for new markets and higher-value products, but neither adjustment is instantaneous.

events.title: Meloni promises to ban burqas, niqabs in Italy’s schools
events.summary: Italy will ban burqas and niqabs in schools, as well as limit the number of foreign students in classes, said far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, with immigration expected to be a central issue in next year’s general election. Meloni outlined the proposed changes on Sunday at a gathering of the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy (FdI) party, adding that they would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign students having “serious difficulties integrating into the school system”. list 1 of 3 Meloni sets a record, leading Italy’s longest-serving government since WWII list 2 of 3 Europe’s far right: Putin’s best friend? list 3 of 3 ‘Anti-Zionism is not anti-Semitism’: Protesters warn against Italian bill “For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules,” she said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. “It is the only serious way to welcome them.” Once approved by the government, the changes would need parliamentary approval within 60 days to pass into law. Meloni’s right-wing administration is Italy’s longest-running government since the end of the Second World War , but her party is expected to face a serious challenge in 2027 from the National Future (FN) party, which is further to the right of the FdI and its popularity has been rapidly increasing in polls since February. FN called for a crackdown on the wearing of burqas in schools in July. Burqas are full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including the eyes. Niqabs are similar, but the eyes are visible. Neither covering is expressly banned in Italy, but a 1975 law prohibits the use of helmets or garments that make identification difficult without a justified reason. A 2008 ruling later clarified that full-face coverings may be worn for religious or cultural reasons if the face is revealed when identity verification is required. However, the anti-immigrant League party, which is part of Meloni’s ruling coalition, submitted a bill earlier this year that would ban helmets or garments, except in specific circumstances such as sporting events or places of worship. Alongside the burqa ban, Meloni said she would implement a legal cap on the number of foreign students per class. However, a 30 percent limit on foreign students per class and school already exists under Italian law and Meloni did not spell out how that would change. events.title: Meta’s Muse TV ad is the latest sign that AI agents are going mainstream
events.summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta released a TV ad for Muse, its personal AI agent, as it pushes AI agents into the mainstream. Muse can act on a user's behalf, sending emails, purchasing things online, and handling other tasks. Fears about AI agents going rogue haven't dissuaded hype about the new tech. The next shiny new AI thing has arrived: The personal AI agent . Once mostly the domain of Silicon Valley coders who used them to amp up their efficiency at work (and anxiety levels ), the AI agent is now being welcomed into the home. And with the release of Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, the do-it-for-you tech is rocketing into the mainstream. "It feels like magic," investor Sheel Mohnot said on X in reference to Instinct, another trendy new personal AI agent . "Contrary to what some people have said, I don't think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types." These agents often live on common messaging apps. Users send messages, asking them to handle tasks like sending emails, purchasing things online, posting to social media, tracking prices, managing calendars, among many other things. In Meta's first television spot, released this weekend, for the Muse AI agent , a woman prepares for a dinner party — chopping lettuce, mixing drinks — while her AI agent autonomously sorts emails, arranges her schedule, and purchases back-to-school items online. "Muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you," Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X on Saturday. muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you this is our first @muse ad ever, going live this weekend! we hope you like it while watching the big game(s)! big ups to @joshginsberg , denise, and the whole meta marketing team ❤️ pic.twitter.com/1zMUVgdKna — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) September 20, 2026 The appeal of autonomous agents is plain. While the famous chatbots from Anthropic and OpenAI that are changing the world are designed to answer questions, personal AI agents can act on a user's behalf, run entirely in the background, handle whole processes online, and ping you with progress updates. It likely won't be long until AI agents are all over the internet. If you really want to take full advantage of their potential, however, Muse and other AI agents require the keys to your kingdom, including your email, your credit card information, your bank accounts, and an array of passwords. "A mistake or manipulation could have real-world consequences, and that is terrifying," Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at internet security firm ESET, recently told Business Insider. Meta has taken pains to reassure users that its agent cares about keeping your information secure. In marketing materials, Meta calls Muse "an agent that respects privacy." So far, concerns about privacy haven't dissuaded consumers from jumping on the personal AI assistant bandwagon. One day after its launch, Muse shot to the top of the App Store. "Introducing Muse," a line of text on the Muse app reads. "AI that hustles for you." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is O n 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “ existential crisis ” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAI misused human work . The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”. This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use their models’ maths prowess as an advertisement . But they rely on mathematicians to check their – often sloppy and baffling – work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment. Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as they commit their names to open letters denouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been a nuanced discussion of how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities. Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematician Nestor Guillen wrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping 's visit to the U.S. this week. "In New York City, Vice Premier He Lifeng and I are continuing our discussions on the U.S.-China economic and trade relationship ahead of [President Donald Trump 's] historic summit with President Xi in Washington," Bessent said in a post to X along with a photo of himself and He.
